wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Priya was twenty-six when the mortar struck the bus station in her hometown, a city that had been under intermittent shelling for weeks. She had been walking home from the market when the air split open. The blast threw her to the ground, and when she looked up, the station was a ruin of twisted metal and smoke. A woman nearby was screaming over a child who lay still. Priya ran toward them, but her hands were useless—she had no training, no bandages, only the sight of blood pooling around the little boy’s head. She could not stop the bleeding. She could not save him. In the months that followed, the memory of that child’s stillness grew into a conviction: she should have done more, she should have protected them, and her failure meant she was fundamentally weak.

Now, six years later, Priya works as a school counselor in a suburban district outside Chicago. She is married to Anil, an engineer, and they live in a quiet apartment complex. But the war zone she left lives inside her, shaped by the appraisals that took root in its aftermath. The belief that she failed to protect others, that she is a weak person, that she is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined her—these three judgments anchor everything she does. She has come to see herself as someone who cannot be trusted in a crisis, someone who folds under pressure. This is why, every morning, she puts on a loose, shapeless cardigan in a muted gray, and pulls her hair into a tight bun at the nape of her neck. The clothing is not about fashion; it is about concealment. She wears it to avoid being noticed, to shrink into the background, because being seen feels like an invitation for others to discover how little she has to offer.

The concealment is one of several strategies she has adopted, each one born from the same desperate logic: if she can control her exposure, she can prevent another failure. She avoids public transport entirely, driving alone to and from school even though the commute strains their budget. The sight of a bus stop—or the hiss of air brakes—drops her straight back into that ruined station, and she is certain she would freeze or panic. She also avoids news reports about any conflict, war, or terrorist attack. When a colleague mentions something happening overseas, she changes the subject or excuses herself. The headlines feel personal: they remind her that other people are suffering while she did nothing, and the guilt that follows is unbearable. Yet these very strategies, which she clings to for safety, only tighten the grip of her negative appraisals. Each time she reaches for the remote to turn off the news, the act confirms to herself that she cannot handle even secondhand reminders of violence—what kind of person is that weak? Each time she drives past a bus stop, she thinks, *See, you can’t even take a normal commute like everyone else.* The avoidance becomes evidence, over and over, that she is no longer capable of a regular life.

At work, the consequences are accumulating. Priya used to enjoy running small group sessions with students, helping them navigate family stress or friendship conflicts. Now she dreads those meetings. A boy in her caseload recently told her he was worried about his uncle who was deployed overseas. Priya felt her chest lock. She gave a generic answer and ended the session early, then spent the rest of the day in her office with the door closed. That evening, she told Anil she didn’t think she was fit for the job anymore. She had once seen herself as a helper, someone who could hold space for others; now she saw only a fraud who could not even listen to a child’s worry without falling apart. The appraisals looped back into her strategies: the next morning, she wore an even larger cardigan, and she took a longer route to school to avoid the one block where a local news van sometimes sits.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment at a school assembly. The principal played a short video about a charity doing relief work in a conflict zone, and the sudden sound of sirens in the clip sent Priya into a dissociative flashback. She did not scream or cry; she simply stood up and walked out, robotically, and sat in her car for forty minutes shaking. The next day she called a therapist. What frightens her most is the possibility that she is right—that she is too weak to have a meaningful life and too broken to ever protect anyone. But a part of her, the part that still wants to be the counselor she once was, hopes that talking about it might loosen the knot.
